name: Hassan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We don't work for companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee on a hydraulic excavator at Tallow Creek, the big gold pit. Basically I sit in a cab the size of a small kitchen and load haul trucks, four passes per truck if you're good, five or six if you're me. Twelve-hour shifts, rotating days and nights. I love the machine, honestly, it's like the biggest toy in the world. What wears me out is nights, and the trainer, Bev, sighing when I miss the truck bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on an excavator?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a forklift at the port warehouse for twenty-five years. Then they brought in robot carts that move the pallets themselves, and at fifty-five I was out, along with forty others. I'd already been watching videos about mining equipment, so I applied here the same month. My wife Leila had surgery last year and our son's food truck went under, and we helped with both, so our savings are basically gone, a few weeks at most. But I'd do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, alright, so it's a tool, like a good calculator. I'd probably post something on the miners' forum I follow, asking what the AI tools are actually good for then. I'm the guy who wants to know how things work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, really. I'd keep using AI the way I do now, to quiz myself on the safety rules and plan my shopping. If AI stays a tool, I'll just be the old man who's weirdly good with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the excavator and try to get signed off as a full operator within the year. I'd keep using the AI to study the machine manuals. And I'd start putting a little away again now that the medical bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by it, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you use AI every day. What does that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it things on my break, like why the hydraulics feel slow when it's cold, and it explains it better than the manual. I record a voice note after shift about what went wrong and ask it for tips. Bev thinks I'm crazy, but my passes are getting quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After the port, does a quiet plateau feel safe to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, not safe. The port taught me that the robot doesn't need to be clever, just cheaper. The carts that replaced us were stupid machines, really. So I'd still keep my eyes open.

S0.say: He'd say AI is just a tool, like a good calculator, and ask on a miners' forum what AI tools are actually good for.
S0.think: He thinks a plateau changes nothing for him: he'd keep using AI to study and plan, and be the older worker who's unusually good with it.
S0.do: Keeps working toward full sign-off on the excavator within a year, using AI to study the manuals. Starts saving again now that the medical bills are paid.
S0.quote: If AI stays a tool, I'll just be the old man who's weirdly good with it.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan has already lost a job to automation and still talks about machines with affection. He uses AI daily in practical ways, recording voice notes after shift to improve. His lesson from the port, that cheap robots don't need to be clever, keeps him watchful even in the calmest picture.

steps.text: Get signed off as a full excavator operator at Tallow Creek within a year
Keep using the AI to study the excavator manuals and safety rules
Start putting a little away again now the medical bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to happen whether we like it or not, so let's be the ones who learn it. At work I'd tell the guys not to wait. I wouldn't blame the robots, I'd blame companies that don't plan for their people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've done this once already, so I'm not as scared as the others. At the port I was angry for a week, then I watched mining videos for a month, then I had a new job. I think I can do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company about the remote operations centre in the first week and sign up for any course. I'd use AI to learn the basics of automation systems in the evenings. If Tallow Creek wasn't training people, I'd look at the other mines that are, even if it means driving further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it risky, with almost no savings, to be the first to jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Leila reminds me. But the risk at the port was not jumping. The guys who waited for the company to look after them were the ones still looking for work two years later. With little money you can't afford to be slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, actually, my trainer. She's sixty, brilliant on the machine, but she won't touch a computer. She's taught me everything and she'd be the one left behind. I'd try to drag her to the course with me.

S1.say: He'd tell co-workers not to wait but to be the ones who learn the new systems, blaming companies that don't plan for their people rather than the robots.
S1.think: He thinks he's less scared than others because he's already rebuilt his working life once, after the port, and believes he can do it again.
S1.do: Asks about the remote operations centre in the first week and signs up for any course, studying automation basics with AI in the evenings. Looks at other mines that train people if his own doesn't, even with a longer drive.
S1.quote: At the port I was angry for a week, then I watched mining videos for a month, then I had a new job.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan's calm comes from experience, not money; he has almost no savings and admits it's risky. His point that thin savings make waiting more dangerous is a neat reversal of what one might expect. He worries most for his trainer Bev, a skilled operator who refuses computers.

steps.text: Ask about the remote operations centre in week one and sign up for courses
Learn the basics of automation systems with AI in the evenings
Look at other mines that train people, even if the drive is longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. So the smart part comes first and the hands later. At the port it was the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the miners' forum I'd post that the remote control rooms are the first jobs to go, so don't retrain for a screen. I'd tell the guys at Tallow Creek that the hands-on work has three more years, and the robots will need people to fix them until then. I'd keep it practical, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared and I'd also be doing sums. In 2028 the computer can plan the pit and run the remote rigs, but my excavator still needs hands on the sticks until about 2031. That's three years, I'd be 63 at the end, and I've got a few weeks of savings. At the port there was another industry to run to, and this time every industry gets the same card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask the maintenance superintendent if I can do a fitter's apprenticeship on the side, even unpaid on my days off. I'd use the AI every night to learn hydraulics and diagnostics, because it'd be brilliant at teaching by 2028. We'd sell the car and use the mine bus, and Leila's part-time wage would cover the food. I'd aim to be the guy who fixes the excavators by 2030, not the guy driving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. It's the port feeling, but this time I see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots that can do hands-on work could fix machines too. Doesn't that close the door in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But the first robots will break, and someone has to know the old machines and the new ones. If I get two or three years as a fitter, that takes me close to my pension. I'm not trying to win forever, just to reach sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Bev, your trainer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev's sixty and won't touch a computer, but she knows the excavator better than anyone alive. I'd tell my trainer Bev to teach the fitters what the machine sounds like before it breaks, because no manual has that. That's worth money for three years.

S2.say: The remote control rooms are the first jobs to go, so don't retrain for a screen. Hands-on work has three more years, and the robots will need people to fix them until then.
S2.think: In 2028 the computer can plan the pit and run the remote rigs, but my excavator needs hands on the sticks until about 2031. I'd be 63 by then with a few weeks of savings, and this time every industry gets the same card.
S2.do: Asks the maintenance superintendent in month one for a fitter's apprenticeship on his days off and studies hydraulics and diagnostics with AI every night. Sells the car for the mine bus, lets Leila's wage cover food, and aims to be fixing excavators by 2030.
S2.feel: Anxious but awake, like the port again, only this time he sees it coming.
S2.quote: At the port there was another industry to run to, and this time every industry gets the same card.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan grasped the new order of events quickly: screen jobs go first, hands-on work follows three years later. He drops the remote-centre plan from the steady scenario and aims for a hands-on fitter role that could carry him close to his pension. He's not trying to win, only to reach sixty-five, and he sees value in his trainer's know-how.

steps.text: Ask for a fitter's apprenticeship on his days off at Tallow Creek
Study hydraulics and diagnostics with the AI every night
Sell the car and take the mine bus to work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. I'd be sixty-six by the robots. Good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the forum I'd say this is the version where people like us can actually plan. Five years to learn, eight before the hands-on work changes. I'd tell the young guys to start a diploma now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. I'd get signed off on the excavator, do a diploma, work a few years as a fitter and retire at sixty-five before the robots arrive. Five years is long enough for me to become the guy who fixes the robot excavator instead of the guy it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in a two-year night diploma in mechatronics, mechanics and electronics together, with AI as my tutor. I'd save something every month to build three months of cushion. And I'd keep working toward full operator sign-off so the pay goes up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit excited, the way I was when I found the mining videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the diploma with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The full operator rate is about a hundred more a week. That pays the diploma, about 800 a year. Leila says I'm always one step ahead of the money, and she's right, but this time the step is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching the new guys how the robot excavator thinks, with a coffee in my hand. Then retiring with Leila and our grandkids, and maybe helping our son start another food truck.

S3.say: This is the version where people like us can actually plan. Five years to learn and eight before hands-on work changes, so start a diploma now.
S3.think: I'd get signed off, do a diploma, work a few years as a fitter and retire at sixty-five before the robots. Five years is long enough to become the guy who fixes the robot excavator instead of the guy it replaces.
S3.do: Enrols in a two-year night diploma in mechatronics with AI as his tutor, paid for by the full operator rate. Saves monthly to build three months of cushion and keeps working toward full operator sign-off.
S3.feel: Calm, mostly, and a little excited, like when he first found the mining videos.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to become the guy who fixes the robot excavator instead of the guy it replaces.
S3.fieldNote: With robots not due until 2034, Hassan's plan fits neatly between now and his pension. He pays for training out of the pay rise from sign-off, a typical small, practical step. His adaptability shows as enjoyment rather than fear here.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year night diploma in mechatronics, about 800 a year
Use the AI as his tutor for the diploma
Save monthly until there's three months of cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039? I'll be retired and teaching my grandkids to drive a forklift for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the forum I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. I'd offer to help anyone learn the new systems. Older guys especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, I'd retire years before. With ten years I could actually enjoy learning the robots instead of running from them. That's never happened to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the excavator sign-off, then do the mechatronics diploma at a normal pace. I'd build about six months of savings. And I'd run a little learning group in the crib room, using AI to make the manuals simple for older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud, like I'd finally got ahead of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why run a learning group if you'll be retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at the port nobody helped the forty of us. I want the older guys at Tallow Creek to have someone who's been through it. Bev might even come, if I bring cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's 33 and cooks, that's hands-on, so he gets the three extra years. I'd tell my son to save from his next food truck, not spend it all on the van.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. I'd help anyone learn the new systems, older guys especially.
S4.think: I'd be fine and retired years before. With ten years I could actually enjoy learning the robots instead of running from them, which has never happened to me.
S4.do: Finishes the excavator sign-off, then does the mechatronics diploma at a normal pace and builds about six months of savings. Runs a learning group in the crib room, using AI to simplify manuals for older workers.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit proud, as if he'd finally got ahead of something.
S4.quote: With ten years I could actually enjoy learning the robots instead of running from them.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets Hassan enjoy the change instead of racing it. Remembering that nobody helped the forty laid-off port workers, he wants to teach older colleagues. He also uses the card's three-year gap to advise his son, who cooks for a living.

steps.text: Finish excavator sign-off, then do the mechatronics diploma at a normal pace
Build about six months of savings
Run a crib-room learning group to help older workers with new systems

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the screen jobs I'd run to go first and the hands-on ones three years later, so there's nowhere to run and not much time to learn. What would help is paid training that starts the day the news hits, open to older workers too, and some money to live on while you learn. And companies that hire the older guys once we've done the training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people like me learned the first time. The robot carts at the port weren't smart. They were cheap and they didn't need lunch, and that was enough. People think it's about clever AI, but cheap is usually enough.

headlineQuote: The robot carts at the port weren't smart. They were cheap and they didn't need lunch, and that was enough.
portrait: Hassan Fischer is 58 and a trainee excavator operator at the Tallow Creek gold pit, a job he took at fifty-five after robot carts replaced him and forty others at a port warehouse. Medical bills and his son's failed food truck have used up his savings, but he loves machines and uses AI every day to learn. Having rebuilt his working life once, he is calm in a plateau and in steady disruption. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because the screen jobs he'd retrain for go first and every industry faces the same card, so he'd aim for a hands-on fitter's role to carry him close to his pension. With five or ten years he plans a night diploma in mechatronics, expects to retire before the robots and wants to help older colleagues learn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the screen jobs he'd retrain for go first, hands-on work follows three years later, and there'd be no other industry to run to.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training from the day the news breaks, open to older workers with money to live on while learning, and companies willing to hire older people afterwards.
